Fictitious means not real — something that has been made up or invented, and does not actually exist.

Think of it this way: if something is fictitious, you cannot find it in the real world. It lives only in someone's imagination, on paper, or in a story — or it was deliberately invented to mislead someone.
The Two Main Ways It's Used

The word "fictitious" works in two closely related but slightly different situations.

1. Something invented for creative or storytelling purposes

When a writer creates a story, the characters, places, and events they invent are fictitious. They don't exist in real life — they were born entirely from imagination.

Examples:

  • "The characters in this novel are entirely fictitious." — The people in the book were made up by the author. They are not based on real, existing individuals.
  • "The story is set in the fictitious town of Millhaven." — There is no such town in reality; the author created it.
  • "The plot involves a fictitious war between two imaginary kingdoms."

In this usage, the word carries no negative judgment. It simply means the thing is invented, not real. There is no blame, no dishonesty — it's just creative invention.

2. Something invented with the intent to deceive

This is where "fictitious" takes on a sharper, more serious edge. Here, it means something has been deliberately fabricated — made up to trick, mislead, or hide the truth from someone.

Examples:

  • "He gave the police a fictitious name." — He lied about his name; the name he gave doesn't belong to him.
  • "The company was built on fictitious financial records." — The financial data was invented to make the company look healthier than it actually was.
  • "She used a fictitious address on her job application." — The address she wrote down doesn't exist or isn't hers; she made it up.
  • "The witness gave a fictitious account of the incident." — What they said didn't actually happen; it was a lie or fabrication.

In this usage, the word carries a negative, serious tone. It implies someone deliberately created a false reality to deceive others, which is often unethical or even illegal.
The Glue That Holds Both Meanings Together

Both uses of the word share one common thread: the thing in question does not exist in reality — it was invented by a human mind. The difference is simply why it was invented:

  • For creativity and storytelling → No negative intent. Think: novels, films, games.
  • For deception and fraud → Negative intent. Think: fake identities, false reports, fabricated claims.

Context will almost always make it clear which meaning is intended.

Understanding a word deeply also means knowing how it sits alongside words that seem similar.

Fictitious vs. Fictional
These two words are very close, and people sometimes use them interchangeably. However, there's a useful difference in practice:

  • Fictional almost always refers to creative works — stories, novels, films. "Harry Potter is a fictional character" is perfect.
  • Fictitious can be used in that creative sense too, but it's also very commonly used in the serious, deceptive sense. You'd more naturally say "he gave a fictitious name" rather than "a fictional name."
  • Think of "fictional" as belonging more to the world of art and storytelling, and "fictitious" as being at home in both storytelling and in formal, legal, or serious contexts where something is being exposed as false.

Fictitious vs. False

  • False simply means not true or not correct. It's a broad word.
  • Fictitious is more specific: it implies the thing was actively invented or constructed by someone. A statement can be false by accident (someone was wrong). But something fictitious was made up — it came from deliberate invention.

Fictitious vs. Fake

  • Fake is more informal and is often used for physical objects or identities (a fake ID, a fake smile).
  • Fictitious is more formal and is better suited to things like names, accounts, entities, reports, or characters.

Fictitious vs. Imaginary

  • Imaginary means something that exists only in the mind, often without any intent to put it into the world or deceive anyone. A child's imaginary friend is imaginary.
  • Fictitious implies the thing has been stated, presented, or represented as something — either in a story or as a deception. It's been given some form, even if that form is false.
Strength and Tone of the Word

"Fictitious" is a formal word. You will see it frequently in:

  • Legal and official documents ("a fictitious business name," "a fictitious claim")
  • Literary criticism and analysis ("a fictitious narrator")
  • News and investigative writing ("the charges were based on fictitious evidence")
  • Academic writing

It is not a casual, everyday word. If you're speaking informally, you'd more likely say "made up," "fake," or "not real." But when precision and formality are needed, "fictitious" is the right tool.
A Simple Test to Check Your Understanding

Ask yourself: "Was this thing invented by someone — either for a story, or to deceive?"

  • If yes → it is fictitious.
  • If no (it's real and genuine) → it is not fictitious.

A real person named John Smith → Not fictitious.
A character named John Smith in a novel → Fictitious.
Someone who falsely tells police their name is John Smith → Fictitious.
Fictitious describes anything that was invented rather than real — whether created imaginatively for storytelling, or fabricated dishonestly to deceive.
